title: Berlin War Damage Still Visible - Quick Summary
items: **The best place to start is a courtyard on Museum Island, and it costs nothing.** The Kolonnadenhof, between the Alte Nationalgalerie and the Neues Museum, has bullet pocks scattered across its columns at roughly the height of a standing person. It is open, paved and never signposted.

**There are three different things to tell apart.** A bullet pock is small, round and clustered. Shell splinter fans outward from one impact point. Heavy weapon damage leaves craters, gouges and pierced steel, and you meet it at the Humboldthain flak tower and under the Prellerweg railway bridge.

**Some of it survived by accident, some of it was kept on purpose.** The Neues Museum is the deliberate case: David Chipperfield’s restoration, finished in 2009, left the holes and rebuilt around them in plain brick and concrete, and it won the Mies van der Rohe Award in 2011.

**The Museum für Naturkunde says all of this on its own building pages.** Bullet holes on the front facade, an east wing completed in flat grey concrete against the surviving stone, and a dome that was never rebuilt after the raid of 3 February 1945.

**Most of the fresh damage dates from about ten days in April 1945.** Soviet units reached the AEG works in Wedding and the flak tower on 26 April, the Gestapo block beside the Gropius Bau on 29 April, and the Stadtbahn viaduct at Friedrichstraße on 30 April and 1 May.

**Two sites need planning.** The Reichstag inscriptions are indoors and need a free registration in advance. The Pergamonmuseum has been shut since 23 October 2023 and its north wing is not due back until 4 June 2027.
